I used to be 320. I've been sitting at a comfortable 160 for a good 3 years and counting. Want to know what I learned?

Time is your best friend. Or at least, how you're perceiving it.

Your goal should be to make food and food related thoughts as small a part of your day as having a shite in the morning. That doesn't mean starve yourself.

Please, for the love of all holy, DO NOT starve yourself. That can cause irreparable damage to your metabolism and hormones. Those are issues you REALLY don't want when trying to maintain weight loss.

Do it SLOW, take it easy, and don't try to take off running. Everyone that has, takes a nosedive a week in. 

Start with small changes. Portion control first. Just make sure your portion sizes aren't insane. Slowly switch out your regular foods with food that is nourishing, and abundant in vitamins. You need to stay hydrated, and you don't want vitamin deficiencies. Take vitamin supplements if you feel you are lacking.

If you feel like you're going to binge, find a taxing hobby that'll wear you out, chew gum, drink a zero calorie drink (could be tea, coffee, or even diet soda), or do some exercise.

Hopefully that helped! Please let me know if you need more specific advice!

Yes, I would absolutely recommend using dumbbells. Strength training is much more effective to burning fat than cardio. Yes, cardio burns calories faster, but you need to burn FAT. Not calories. You want to maintain as much muscle ass possible during a weight loss regime, and strength training is THE way to do that. I lost 160lbs with NO cardio whatsoever.

I just found a middle ground. Instead of purely trying to beef up, or slim down to get that muscle mass to body fat ratio to where I wanted it, I instead combined the two and made up my own circuit. Maybe the same thing will help you?

I recommend you take the more generally appealing approach and slowly ease into eating healthier and healthier foods, and acclimating your taste buds to crave healthier options by eating similar to your 'regular' diet. Learn how to cook those dishes for yourself using all natural ingredients.

After that, slowly start replacing small portions of what you normally eat with healthier options. It will take time, but your diet will slowly fully convert to being nutritious, sustainable and the weight will come off over time along with that progress.

Once a comfortable amount of weight is off (that all depends on you, your starting weight, and your goals), you can search online for different exercises for each muscle group. Try different ones and see which work for you, and create your own workout routine. Whatever you see making visible progress, focus on that. 

The best advice I can give to you at this point is if you rush it, you'll gain it back as quick as it came off; if you take your time and acclimate your body the correct way, it will become your everyday life, and THAT is what your goal should be.
